articles.title: EXCLUSIVE! Author Fiona Davis Dishes on Bringing American Girl to an Adult Audience with Samantha: The Next Chapter
articles.content: If you were a child of the 1980s or later and played with dolls, chances are you owned—or wished for—an American Girl. There was Colonial-era Felicity, and Addy, who grew up during the Civil War, as well as bespectacled Molly, who dated back to World War II, and many more. Far from being just dolls, they had historical backstories, complete with books to go with them, and authentic clothing and accessories that were (and still are) as colorful as their lives. Believe it or not, the burgeoning brand—which was acquired by Mattel in 1998 and has since spawned an empire—is celebrating is 40th anniversary this year. And American Girl is marking the occasion with a new venture: Samantha: The Next Chapter, the first American Girl novel for adults. Yes, you read that right! But the delicious nostalgia is only the beginning. The story, set in New York City circa 1920, centers on the now-grown Samantha Parkington, an aspiring suffragist encouraging other young women to vote in their first presidential election. Her otherwise comfortable life takes an abrupt left turn when her inheritance is stolen and she sets out to save her family’s legacy. Adding to the fun? Fiona Davis, the bestselling author of The Stolen Queen, The Address and The Lions of Fifth Avenue, wrote the book and brought her expertise in New York–based historical fiction to the world of American Girl. We caught up with Davis just before the book’s launch to find out how she created grown-up Samantha’s story and why she thinks American Girl resonates with readers of all ages. Join the free Reader’s Digest Book Club for great reads, monthly discussions, author Q&As and a community of book lovers. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Reader’s Digest: What is your connection to American Girl? Were you a fan of the American Girl dolls or books growing up? Fiona Davis: I was in college when the first book came out, and I don’t have any kids of my own. Where I really connected with American Girl was through my nieces. My brother has three daughters, and all three loved American Girl, especially my niece, Erin. She loved Samantha best and the fact that she was very forward. Erin was shy, so having a doll whose character spoke her mind was very helpful for Erin, who was learning how to find her own voice. Reader’s Digest: How did you end up writing an American Girl book for adults? Fiona Davis: The company approached me and asked if I would write a book around Samantha. In a way, it was a gift not to know a lot about her because otherwise, I would have been paralyzed with fear. She is so loved, and the nostalgia around American Girl and Samatha is so strong. I think I was chosen because I know New York well. I write about historic New York, and the heroines in my stories are all very strong-willed. It was a good match that way. American Girl’s Janelle [Asselin] was my editor for the whole project and was brilliant. She reached out to me by email, which I reported to my agent and asked her if she thought it was a scam. She called them and said it was the real thing. So it all happened pretty quickly, and we were soon off to the races. Reader’s Digest: Was Samantha a departure from other characters you’ve written about? Fiona Davis: Samantha is a 25-year-old character, and I’ve had main characters who are around that same age as well. I had also worked on projects based in the 1920s. The fact that Samantha is very much into suffrage, even as a young girl, worked well because I had co-edited a group of short stories (Stories from Suffragette City) set around the suffrage parade in New York City in 1915; I have done a lot of research around that. On top of that, the town that Samantha grew up in is based on Mount Kisco, New York, which I know well. Reader’s Digest: Who decided Samantha would be the first adult American Girl to be featured in an adult novel? Fiona Davis: American Girl, the company, was very specific that Samantha would be the first. She was one of the first original dolls. Reader’s Digest: Did you read any of the original American Girl books while preparing? What was that experience like as an adult? Fiona Davis: I did a deep dive because the books are so important to her background. They introduce her family, her extended family, her community, her interests. It was really fun—and a gift not to have to make all that up. As an author, it was wonderful to have it right on the page and then see where it could go. Reading these books as an adult was enlightening; I wish I’d had them as a young girl. The sense of history comes through with such clarity. The characters are so wonderful. Reader’s Digest: Did any other American Girl stories really resonate with you? Fiona Davis: I also loved reading Addy’s story. I like the fact that the books don’t shy away from a difficult era in American history. But Samantha was my focus, for sure. Reader’s Digest: Did anything from this story speak to you on a more personal level? Fiona Davis: My parents are both English, so all our relatives lived in England. We lived in America since I was 3. Even though Samantha had lost her parents and was an orphan, she had such a loving extended family around her. I would have loved to have read these books as young child and experience the idea of having an extended family; I didn’t have that myself. Reader’s Digest: Was there a moment during the writing process when you felt especially aware of the full-circle nature of this project? Fiona Davis: I think it’s wonderful being able to reach beyond the original generation it was intended for. What’s interesting to me is whenever I have met an adult who knows the story, they get so excited. They always know where their American Girl doll is. It might be in their mother’s attic or their basement, and they always say, “Oh, yes, I’m a Samantha” or “I’m a Kirsten.” They identify so closely with the dolls and their characters. Reader’s Digest: Was it difficult adapting a character that so many people grew up with? Fiona Davis: The real challenge was staying true to her character as a child. Samantha is empathetic, tenacious and very intelligent. We needed to make sure that during all the stages—the research, writing and editing—that Samantha’s inner strength was still present. Meanwhile, she is an adult, having adult experiences. Readers need to know who the character is at her core and recognize that. Also, as a character, I had to have her undergo growth, so in the story, she’s maybe a little bit different than when she started. It’s the first time I’ve been handed a character and told to write a book about her. Reader’s Digest: This book will be such a hugely nostalgic story for a lot of readers. When crafting it, how did you balance nostalgia with telling a rich, complex story your way? Fiona Davis: I was lucky that I had a team of people behind me as I wrote. They not only included my editor but also a historian on staff at American Girl who supplied me with everything I needed to stay true to the time period. On top of that, they have a panel of consultants and experts and advisors on whatever subjects we were dealing with who could weigh in and make sure that the story was true to history. Their contributions are on every page of that book. I think that because it was this wonderful team effort, we carried that balance of nostalgia and growth throughout the plot. Reader’s Digest: Why do you think American Girl has such a lasting impact on so many of us? Fiona Davis: It’s because the American Girl team really cares about how the characters come across. They understand that they are affecting young girls, and there’s a huge responsibility there that they take very seriously. I think people who buy American Girl dolls understand that. That is why there is such brand loyalty. I think customers understand they are not being talked down to. The early stories are so fun to read, no matter what age you are. There’s a common thread throughout American Girl, no matter which character you identify with. With this book, the way I like to describe it is like going on a long road trip with an old friend. It’s somewhere new, but you have an old friend by your side the whole way. At Reader’s Digest, we’ve been sharing our favorite books for over 100 years. articles.title: King Charles and Queen Camilla’s Nighttime Ritual Is Surprisingly Sweet
articles.content:
The relationship between Charles and Camilla, the king and queen of England, has been under a microscope for decades. Charles’s first wife, Princess Diana, who died in 1997, was pretty uniformly beloved, and Camilla was … well, let’s just say it took the public some time to warm up to her.
But despite how things went down all those years ago, it’s become clear that Charles and Camilla absolutely adore each other. They laugh at the same things, as she revealed last year on the couple’s 20th anniversary, and they enjoy spending time together even when they are like two “ships passing in the night,” as she told British Vogue a few years ago.
It makes one wonder why they didn’t just marry each other right off the bat, but that’s a whole other story. And everyone deserves happiness, right? Now, in a new documentary, the queen is opening up about a nighttime ritual that she shares with her husband, and it is so sweet and relatable, you might almost forget they’re royalty. Read on to learn what these two do to keep the love alive.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more royal news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
Like a lot of couples, the king and queen read together every night. She divulged their charming routine in a new BBC documentary called The Book That Changed My Life. The documentary was produced in partnership with the Open University and Camilla’s charity, the Queen’s Reading Room, as part of the U.K.’s National Year of Reading.
“My husband and I actually read before dinner,” Camilla told the BBC. “We just like sitting quietly and reading.”
The queen went on to paint a picture of domesticity for the royal pair, describing how reading and their pre-dinner ritual are incredibly important to her. “It’s part of our heritage. If there’s no reading, personally, we might as well all give up,” Camilla said. “Because I don’t think we’d even be human anymore.”
He’s apparently not one to stay silent when reading, much to the queen’s dismay. “I, occasionally, when I’m deep in a book, hear him roaring with laughter about something,” Camilla said in the doc. “It’s very off-putting. I can’t get back into my book, or I’ll suddenly start weeping. But it’s a lovely, quiet time.”
She chalks up this quirk to the fact that Charles enjoys reading P.G. Wodehouse, the famed British humorist behind literary characters such as the quintessential English butler, Jeeves, and his employer, Bertie Wooster. Camilla, meanwhile, prefers thrillers and historical fiction, which aren’t exactly known for their laugh-a-minute hilarity.
Very. She points to her own early life spent reading and how it set her up for success when opportunities were limited. “I left school quite young, because in my day, women didn’t go to university,” Camilla said. “I think reading has been most of my education.”
The queen credits her father, Bruce Shand, with instilling a love of reading in her. “We must’ve been very, very young when my father started reading to us,” she said. “I think that’s where my love of reading came from.” She recalled reading Treasure Island and Peter Pan before graduating to A Tale of Two Cities, which she said coincided with her childhood fascination with the guillotine!
“I don’t think our childhood would have been the same if we didn’t have books,” she told the BBC.
The Queen’s Reading Room, which began as a book club during the COVID-19 pandemic and now reaches 12 million people in 183 countries, is an extension of her love of reading. But it’s about more than that: The Queen’s Reading Room also funds neuroscience research to study how reading and well-being are connected, and partners with other charities to provide books to people in the hospital or experiencing homelessness or domestic abuse.

articles.title: Attention, Annoying Humans: You Might Be Interrupting Your Dog’s Sleep, According to a New Study
articles.content:
My sweet dog Willie Nelson is in his golden years—that long stretch of vaguely declining health and general slowing down that every pet parent braces for. Every night, he “jumps” (or, more often, is lifted) onto the bed and we snuggle in for a good night’s sleep filled with his snoring and snorting and kicking and rearranging … until I get up around 3 a.m. and move to the guest room.
Yes, sleeping with our pets can be problematic. But I would never kick him out: It’s not Willie’s fault I’m a light sleeper, and it took us forever to haul him up on the bed in the first place. And now, a new study confirms that co-sleeping has its downsides—not necessarily for you, but for your dog.
Ahead, I’ll take you through the results of this new research that totally upends what we think we know about humans, dogs and sleep. Read on to learn how your sleeping arrangements might be affecting everyone in your family, furry members included.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more pet news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
Yes, we are, according to new research by scientists at the University of Toronto Mississauga. The study, which was published in Plos One, was on the small side, but it looked at 25 human participants and their 38 canine counterparts to find out how sleep patterns were affected by co-sleeping.
To do this, researchers outfitted dogs and owners with sleep monitors, and found that 61% of the subject “dyads” (aka the individual pairs of humans and dogs studied) moved together at some point in the night. But of that majority of interspecies co-sleepers who were in tandem, it was usually the human who moved first—not the dog.
Yep, in nearly half (45%) of the dyads that showed movement, it was the person who was doing the disturbing first. Could my dog, Willie, be off the hook for my banishment to the spare bedroom? I don’t quite believe it, but researchers have some pretty good numbers to back it up.
They measured both objective activity levels (using sleep monitors) and subjective variables, including the perception of sleep quality (which unfortunately our dogs can’t answer). They found that our belief that Fido is preventing us from sleeping, and not the other way around, might be a misperception, though the authors say more study is needed.
Researchers didn’t come to any conclusions about how these results could be affecting our animals. But as any of us who have been roused out of our REM cycle in the middle of the night—only to stare at the ceiling, attempt to count sheep or give up and read a book—can attest, lack of sleep is bad for you and, presumably, your dog too.
Sleep studies in dogs aren’t too common, but 2022 research published in Animals found that dogs who got less than eight to 10 hours of sleep were more likely to receive a higher “problem behavior score” by their owners. A 2025 study in Scientific Reports found that sleep can affect learning in dogs under certain situations, and an earlier one from 2017, published in the same journal, reported that dogs learn while sleeping, just like people do.
So given what we know about how important sleep is for humans, combined with this new data on dogs, it seems logical to conclude that sleep disruptions could be affecting their overall well-being, similar to how they affect ours. But sleep in dogs is still a relatively untapped field of study, so take everything with a grain of salt.
My anecdotal evidence aside, apparently not. Researchers in this study found that among the majority of participants whose sleep moves correlated with their dogs’ movements, the dogs moved first only 18% of the time. (Compare that with the 45% of the time we prompt movement in our pups.)
And when it came to objectively measured sleep patterns, like sleep duration and sleep efficiency in humans and overall nighttime activity in dogs, co-sleeping had no effect on either party. In the subjective measurements, humans reported poorer sleep only when they had more than one dog, even though the objective measurements didn’t back up their assumptions.

My sweet dog Willie Nelson is in his golden years—that long stretch of vaguely declining health and general slowing down that every pet parent braces for. Every night, he “jumps” (or, more often, is lifted) onto the bed and we snuggle in for a good night’s sleep filled with his snoring and snorting and kicking and rearranging … until I get up around 3 a.m. and move to the guest room.

Yes, sleeping with our pets can be problematic. But I would never kick him out: It’s not Willie’s fault I’m a light sleeper, and it took us forever to haul him up on the bed in the first place. And now, a new study confirms that co-sleeping has its downsides—not necessarily for you, but for your dog.

Ahead, I’ll take you through the results of this new research that totally upends what we think we know about humans, dogs and sleep. Read on to learn how your sleeping arrangements might be affecting everyone in your family, furry members included.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more pet news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.

Are we really interrupting our dogs’ beauty rest?

Yes, we are, according to new research by scientists at the University of Toronto Mississauga. The study, which was published in Plos One, was on the small side, but it looked at 25 human participants and their 38 canine counterparts to find out how sleep patterns were affected by co-sleeping.

To do this, researchers outfitted dogs and owners with sleep monitors, and found that 61% of the subject “dyads” (aka the individual pairs of humans and dogs studied) moved together at some point in the night. But of that majority of interspecies co-sleepers who were in tandem, it was usually the human who moved first—not the dog.

Yep, in nearly half (45%) of the dyads that showed movement, it was the person who was doing the disturbing first. Could my dog, Willie, be off the hook for my banishment to the spare bedroom? I don’t quite believe it, but researchers have some pretty good numbers to back it up.

They measured both objective activity levels (using sleep monitors) and subjective variables, including the perception of sleep quality (which unfortunately our dogs can’t answer). They found that our belief that Fido is preventing us from sleeping, and not the other way around, might be a misperception, though the authors say more study is needed.

Could this be a problem for our pups?

Researchers didn’t come to any conclusions about how these results could be affecting our animals. But as any of us who have been roused out of our REM cycle in the middle of the night—only to stare at the ceiling, attempt to count sheep or give up and read a book—can attest, lack of sleep is bad for you and, presumably, your dog too.

Sleep studies in dogs aren’t too common, but 2022 research published in Animals found that dogs who got less than eight to 10 hours of sleep were more likely to receive a higher “problem behavior score” by their owners. A 2025 study in Scientific Reports found that sleep can affect learning in dogs under certain situations, and an earlier one from 2017, published in the same journal, reported that dogs learn while sleeping, just like people do.

So given what we know about how important sleep is for humans, combined with this new data on dogs, it seems logical to conclude that sleep disruptions could be affecting their overall well-being, similar to how they affect ours. But sleep in dogs is still a relatively untapped field of study, so take everything with a grain of salt.

Are dogs interrupting our sleep too?

My anecdotal evidence aside, apparently not. Researchers in this study found that among the majority of participants whose sleep moves correlated with their dogs’ movements, the dogs moved first only 18% of the time. (Compare that with the 45% of the time we prompt movement in our pups.)

And when it came to objectively measured sleep patterns, like sleep duration and sleep efficiency in humans and overall nighttime activity in dogs, co-sleeping had no effect on either party. In the subjective measurements, humans reported poorer sleep only when they had more than one dog, even though the objective measurements didn’t back up their assumptions.

Interestingly, dogs that slept in the same room with their humans but not on the same bed were more likely to disrupt their owners’ sleep. Overall, researchers note the need for larger, more robust studies of dog-and-human sleep patterns. Willie and I will wait eagerly for this emerging research, but one thing I can tell you is that he’s not moving.

Being related to someone who came over on the Mayflower seems like one of those things that’s easy to claim but hard to back up. Or is it?
When I got this assignment, I immediately picked up my phone and called my aunt, our family’s resident genealogist, who not only confirmed that we are indeed descended from people on the Mayflower but also rattled off the exact two passengers and their entire long line of rather prodigious offspring—right down to my dad and her.
And we are not alone by any stretch of the imagination. The same two people who spawned my family also have their DNA tentacles in millions of Americans to this very day, from former U.S. presidents to famous actors and artists to little old nobodies like me … and maybe you.
Ahead, Neil Fraser, a partner at London’s Fraser and Fraser, one of the world’s top genealogy firms, and Eva Holmes, the director of the Silver Books Project at the General Society of Mayflower Descendants, give us the history of the Mayflower descendants and explain how to find out if you have any connection to this storied boat.

“The Mayflower carried 102 passengers, including religious Separatists who had previously left England for the Netherlands before being unsettled and planning transport to America via England,” Fraser says. “The Separatists were unhappy with the direction of the Church of England and wanted the freedom to practice their religious beliefs.”
Not everyone was so ideologically bent, though. Fraser says in addition to the Separatists, the Mayflower carried more than 20 crew members and several tradespeople and servants who were hoping for a better life.
“The overcrowded Mayflower set off alone from Plymouth [in England] in 1620 and landed in Cape Cod 66 days later,” Fraser says. “They arrived in modern-day Massachusetts in the midst of winter without shelter or supplies, and around half died during the first winter alone.”
“The Mayflower Society reckons that around 10 million Americans and 35 million people worldwide are descended from passengers on the ship,” Fraser says. You may have heard that 10% of the American population has Mayflower ties, but that’s a misconception. The current population of the U.S. is just under 350 million people, so 10 million descendants would be less than 3%.

But it’s important to remember that in 400 years, there would be an “enormous number of branches on a family tree, and not all of them will have been researched or properly documented,” Fraser says. Over that many generations, records are bound to get lost, and many people just have no idea they’re related to Mayflower passengers, “so I don’t think anyone could give you an exact number.”
“This is the interesting bit,” Fraser says. “Imagine a single Mayflower couple had three children who survived and went on to have families, and each subsequent generation averaged three children who reproduced.” Through 13 generations, they’d have about 2.4 million descendants, and by generation No. 16, we’d be looking at a total of more than 64 million descendants from that single couple!
Of course, not many families reproduce quite so exponentially, but it gives you a good idea of how fast the numbers can grow. You also have to take into account the fact that family trees rarely stay isolated. “Over 400 years, cousins married cousins, sometimes without knowing they were related,” Fraser says. “The same ancestor can therefore appear in multiple branches of a family tree.”
“The remarkable feature of genealogy is that descendants multiply across generations, but family trees overlap,” Fraser adds. “Someone alive today might descend from [Mayflower passenger] John Alden through five or six different lines and from several other Mayflower passengers as well.” This overlapping is called pedigree collapse, “and it is especially relevant to early colonial New England, where relatively small communities intermarried over generations.”

John Howland was a servant who was nearly killed on the voyage, and Elizabeth Tilley was a teenager whose parents both died during the first winter at Plymouth, leaving her an orphan. They eventually married and had 10 children and 88 grandchildren, Fraser says.

So start with your own branch on the family tree. Write down everything you know about your parents, aunts and uncles, grandparents and so on, focusing on names, dates, places and relationships. Ask your relatives, especially older ones, for any documents they have. Look on the backs of old photos for names and dates, and catalog newspaper clippings, military records, naturalization documents, and birth, marriage and death certificates.
“Census returns, wills, parish registers, land records and local archives can all help establish family connections,” Fraser says. “Wills are particularly useful because they often identify children and other relatives, sometimes providing the evidence needed to link one generation to another.”
